title: Tradeweb Government Bond Update – September 2026
summary: Global government bonds sold off for a third consecutive month in September, as higher energy prices, heavy debt issuance and a series of central bank policy decisions weighed on markets. body_markdown:
Global government bonds sold off for a third consecutive month in September, as higher energy prices, heavy debt issuance and a series of central bank policy decisions weighed on markets. Yields on many 10-year benchmark bonds rose by at least 25 basis points over the month, with the French 10-year yield ending the month 67 basis points higher at 4.84%. Preliminary data from statistics agency INSEE showed that annual inflation accelerated to 3.0% in September, from 2.4% in August.


In Germany, annual inflation accelerated to 3.3% in September, from 2.9% the previous month. The 10-year Bund yield rose 26 basis points to 3.58%, and its Italian equivalent climbed nearly 49 basis points to 4.63%. Preliminary data from Istat showed that Italian inflation accelerated to 4.2% in September, from 3.3% in August. At its September meeting, the European Central Bank raised its deposit rate by 25 basis points to 2.5% and reiterated its commitment to ensuring that inflation stabilises at its 2% target over the medium term.


By contrast, the Bank of England left the Bank Rate unchanged at 3.75% and set out a multi-year path for unwinding the government bond holdings accumulated through quantitative easing. Data released by the Office for National Statistics on September 16 showed that the Consumer Prices Index rose by 3.1% in the 12 months to August 2026, its highest level in five months. The 10-year Gilt yield increased 35 basis points to end September at 5.41%. Sweden’s Riksbank also maintained its policy rate at 1.75%, but signalled that increases could begin later this year. The country’s 10-year benchmark bond yield rose 14 basis points to close at 3.23% on September 30.


Across the Atlantic, the Bank of Canada held its target for the overnight rate at 2.25%, with the Bank Rate at 2.5% and the deposit rate at 2.20%. The country’s 10-year government bond yield rose 17.5 basis points to 3.91%. Its U.S. Treasury equivalent increased by more than 41 basis points to 5.16%, reaching levels last seen in 2007. On September 16, the Federal Open Market Committee unanimously voted to raise the target range for the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 3.75%–4.00%. Headline inflation remained at 3.4% in August, still above the Federal Reserve’s 2% target.


**Casey Costanza, U.S. Treasuries Product Manager at Tradeweb** , said: “U.S. Treasuries saw a sharp sell-off in September. After reaching a monthly low of 4.73% on September 3, the 10-year yield climbed 50 basis points to a monthly high of 5.23% on September 25, before retreating modestly into month-end. The move came as the Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time since 2023 and signalled that another increase may follow this year.”


In Asia Pacific, Australia’s 10-year benchmark bond yield rose 24 basis points to 5.35%, after reaching a three-year high of 5.46% on September 28. The Reserve Bank of Australia raised its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.6% on September 29, its fourth increase of the year and the highest level since 2011. Amid ongoing inflationary pressures, the Bank of Japan also raised its policy rate to 1.25% and indicated that further increases could follow, depending on developments in economic activity and prices. The Japanese 10-year government bond yield rose 12.5 basis points to end the month at 3.06%.
